Analytic regularity for convolution equations

Author: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI).

A Fourier multiplier can recover analytic regularity in a direction if its inverse operation has a holomorphic extension of polynomial growth in a complex cone. This criterion applies to convolution by a tempered distribution, including kernels that are neither compactly supported nor differential operators. We prove the directional estimate, account for the noncompact part of the forcing, and then extend the result to convolutions defined by proper addition of supports.

The exact earlier proofs are Continuing the spherical kernel, Lemmas 1–3, for its entire spherical exponential and complex lower bound; Holomorphic decompositions of tempered distributions, Theorem 3, for the spherical representation; and Boundary regularity and conic decomposition, Theorem 3, for its analytic boundary test. Analytic parametrices and straight characteristics, Lemma 1, supplies the coordinate contour identity. Holomorphic boundaries and analytic directions, Theorem 2, proves the full-cone wavefront bound, and Holomorphic boundaries in convex cones, Section 3 and Theorem 3.2, proves polydisk estimates and uniqueness from a zero boundary.

We also use the analytic projection and sum rules in Cones and derivative-growth wavefronts, Theorems 5–7; the analytic convolution inclusion in Keeping zero covectors in kernel operations, Corollary 7; and the proper-support pairing in Convolution as addition of supports, Theorem 1.1. Fourier inversion and transpose conventions are fixed in the Fourier foundation, F1–F5. These supplied programme proofs, together with the arguments below, are the mathematical prerequisites.

The analytic power-series criterion is Derivative growth and finite-order localization, Proposition 3. The half-plane logarithm and its square root are supplied by Complex powers at a boundary, Lemma H0, using .

Exercise 6 (foundation: why growth is part of the hypothesis). Give a convolution that makes every compact input analytic but whose formal reciprocal fails (1).

Solution. Take The Gaussian Fourier identity and normalization are proved in the Fourier foundation. The Gaussian is entire in the complex variable , and pairing its translates with a compact distribution gives an entire function: finite test-order bounds justify all complex derivatives on compact parameter sets. Thus is analytic for every compact . But (1) would force on its real cone, already violating polynomial growth there. In particular is singular while is analytic. Nonvanishing on real frequencies alone cannot replace the full condition.
